records.title: Gene therapy for epilepsy: From SCN1A to broadened therapeutic horizons (Review).
records.abstract: Genetic epilepsy, for which the molecular mechanisms are relatively well defined in numerous monogenic forms, represents an attractive model for the transition from symptomatic seizure control to mechanism‑driven correction. However, gene therapy strategies differ in their mechanisms of action, adaptability to specific mutations and translational maturity, making rational selection of interventions based on variant‑specific functional consequences an important clinical challenge. The present review examined five nucleic acid‑based therapeutic strategies, namely gene supplementation, enhancement of endogenous gene expression, gene silencing, DNA editing and RNA editing, for major causative genes, using mutation‑specific functional consequences [loss‑of‑function (LOF) vs. gain‑of‑function] as the primary framework for therapeutic decision‑making. The mechanisms and suitability of each approach are analysed, and their performance in terms of cell‑type specificity, delivery vectors and safety is evaluated by integrating evidence from animal models, induced pluripotent stem cell‑derived neurons and organoids and clinical trials. The present review also summarised key translational barriers, including vector cargo constraints, blood‑brain barrier penetration, off‑target and immune‑associated risks, therapeutic dosing windows and the timing of developmental intervention. Antisense oligonucleotides and regulatory adeno‑associated viral approaches, supported by mature delivery platforms and manageable safety profiles, have progressed furthest towards clinical validation. Endogenous gene activation strategies, such as CRISPR activation, offer a gene replacement‑free approach for LOF disorders but remain preclinical. DNA and RNA editing, while potentially capable of durable disease modification, require further evidence on delivery efficiency and long‑term homeostatic safety. Gene therapy for genetic epilepsy is undergoing a key transition from proof‑of‑concept studies to individualised clinical application. Future progress will depend on integrating personalised intervention design, multi‑target therapeutic combinations, artificial intelligence‑assisted sequence optimisation and standardised translational models, with the potential to drive a paradigm shift from seizure suppression to mechanistic correction.

records.title: Transplanted human photoreceptors differentially survive, incorporate, and mature in mildly and severely degenerated mouse retinae.
records.abstract: Photoreceptor transplantation is considered a disease-agnostic therapeutic strategy for retinal degenerative diseases with highly heterogeneous genetic, molecular, and cellular pathologies. While integration of human photoreceptors enriched from stem-cell-derived retinal organoids was noted in previous preclinical studies, the potential influence of retinal degeneration severity on transplantation efficiency has not been systematically assessed. Here, we employed mice presenting mild or severe retinal degeneration as recipients for human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived photoreceptors. Donor cells formed multicellular clusters that started to interact with Müller glia processes from 3 weeks post transplantation (wpt) in mildly degenerated retinae, resulting in structural integration and maturation, characterized by inner/outer segment and synapse formation by 26 wpt. In contrast, in severely degenerated hosts, donor photoreceptors remained mainly scattered and showed limited incorporation or signs of maturation. Differential maturation of donor cells in mild vs. severe hosts was confirmed by single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis. However, transplantation at the beginning of the degeneration process of the severe model allowed structural integration and maturation of donor photoreceptors despite complete loss of endogenous photoreceptors over time. The study thus shows that survival, integration, and maturation of donor photoreceptors depend on the degenerative retinal microenvironment shaping significantly the transplantation efficiency.

records.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
records.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

records.title: Establishment and functional evaluation of a two-stage mouse hepatocyte-derived organoid culture system.
records.abstract: Primary hepatocytes rapidly lose differentiated functions during prolonged in vitro culture, limiting their use in studies of liver metabolism and zonation. This study aimed to establish a two-stage mouse hepatocyte-derived organoid system that enables serial cell propagation followed by partial recovery of hepatic identity and metabolic function in three-dimensional culture. Primary mouse hepatocytes were first expanded in a two-dimensional transition and expansion medium and then transferred to low-attachment plates for three-dimensional culture in hepatocyte maturation medium. Cell growth, senescence, organoid formation, hepatic marker expression, bulk transcriptomic changes, albumin secretion, urea production, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, zonation-related responses, and post-cryopreservation recovery were evaluated. Statistical comparisons were performed using ordinary one-way or two-way analysis of variance, as appropriate. The expansion medium supported serial propagation, maintained albumin expression, increased the proportion of Ki67-positive cells, and reduced senescence. A seeding density of 3 × 104 cells per well produced compact and uniform organoids. Following transfer to 3D culture, organoids expressed albumin, E-cadherin, CYP2E1, and CK19. Bulk transcriptomic analysis showed strong cell-cycle activity in passage-2 cells, followed by partial recovery of hepatic metabolic programs during 3D culture, including cholesterol biosynthesis, the urea cycle, steroid biosynthesis, and bile-acid biosynthesis. Direct comparison with freshly isolated primary hepatocytes showed that albumin secretion remained lower than the primary hepatocytes level, whereas urea production increased during 3D culture and was not significantly different from PHCs by day 16. Exposure to 5% oxygen increased lipid-droplet accumulation. Glucose and insulin increased free and total cholesterol. Wnt/R-spondin increased the pericentral-associated marker glutamine synthetase, whereas ascorbic acid and bilirubin increased the periportal-associated marker CPS1. Early-passage cells retained organoid-forming capacity after cryopreservation and recovery. This two-stage culture system supports serial hepatocyte propagation followed by partial and function-specific recovery of hepatic identity and function in 3D culture. Although the organoids did not fully reproduce the mature primary hepatocyte state or physiological liver zonation, the system provides an experimentally accessible in vitro platform for investigating hepatocyte expansion, partial hepatic maturation, metabolic regulation, zonation-related responses, and microenvironment-dependent modulation of hepatocyte function.

records.title: Mapping the subcellular pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic landscape: a systems-pharmacology framework for predicting combination therapies against intracellular bacterial infections.
records.abstract: Intracellular bacterial pathogens represent one of the most formidable challenges in contemporary medicine. By exploiting host cellular niches, these organisms evade immune surveillance and withstand conventional antibiotic therapies, establishing persistent reservoirs that are difficult to eradicate. Although antibiotic combinations, host-directed interventions, and drug repurposing have shown promise, conventional discovery pipelines rarely capture the dynamic and compartmentalized nature of the intracellular environment. This review proposes a systems pharmacology framework centered on subcellular pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Sub-PK/PD) profiling to predict and optimize intracellular combination therapies. Mechanistic and translational studies of intracellular drug disposition, host-pathogen metabolism, computational combination design, and biomimetic infection models were synthesized in a targeted narrative review. Particular attention was given to spatially resolved measurements, dual ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, metabolic flux analysis, machine learning, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Pathogen-containing vacuoles, phagolysosomes, the host cytosol, lipid-rich macrophages, and tissue lesions impose distinct barriers to drug ionization, accumulation, stability, and target engagement. Persistent infection also produces reciprocal metabolic rewiring: host pathways supply carbon, nitrogen, lipids, metals, and reducing equivalents, while bacterial stress programs alter growth and antibiotic susceptibility. Integrating these processes can reveal shared metabolic bottlenecks suitable for combinations of pathogen-directed and host-directed agents. Computational models can prioritize combinations, but their predictions require validation under physiologically realistic concentration-time profiles. Linking systems biology to localized Sub-PK/PD provides a practical roadmap for designing niche-specific regimens. Such regimens could improve clearance of persistent intracellular reservoirs, reduce ineffective exposure, and limit the emergence of antimicrobial resistance.

records.title: Single-cell perturbation prediction near experimental reproducibility with GENESIS.
records.abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases now measure cellular responses across millions of cells, but the number of possible combinations of biological contexts, perturbations, doses and other experimental variables make exhaustive measurements infeasible. Here, we present GENESIS (Generative ENErgy-based Single-cell Intervention Simulator), a generative framework that predicts single-cell response distributions directly from the covariates defining an experimental condition. GENESIS uses a lightweight neural network trained with the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule for distributions. We introduce an experiment-calibrated evaluation framework in which prediction error is interpreted relative to the reproducibility of repeated measurements of the same condition. Across the Tahoe-100M small-molecule atlas and a large PBMC cytokine atlas, GENESIS significantly outperforms existing generative models and statistical baselines and approaches experimental reproducibility on independently repeated conditions. Importantly, GENESIS remains accurate when trained on only a fraction of the available experimental conditions or cells, and generated profiles recover experimentally observed context-dependent transcriptional programs. At comparable training-cell budgets, GENESIS achieves more accurate predictions when measurements span more experimental conditions rather than profiling fewer conditions more deeply. Together, these findings suggest a complementary strategy for perturbation studies: broader, lower-depth measurements can expand experimental coverage, while GENESIS augments sparsely sampled populations and predicts responses in unmeasured conditions.

records.title: MultiFlow: coupled flow matching for predicting single-cell multiomic perturbation responses in unseen cellular contexts.
records.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbation requires resolving coordinated changes across molecular layers, yet most single-cell perturbation models focus on transcriptional responses alone. Here we present MultiFlow, a coupled flow-matching framework that unifies generation and perturbation prediction of paired gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Through bidirectional information exchange between RNA and ATAC generative flows, MultiFlow learns how their joint distribution depends on cellular context and perturbation identity. Across multiomic generation benchmarks, MultiFlow accurately reproduced paired RNA-ATAC states and their population distributions. In multiome perturbation benchmarks, MultiFlow achieved the strongest overall performance in predicting both gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility perturbation responses, outperforming modality-specific perturbation-prediction methods in cell types whose perturbed states were withheld from training. Joint multiomic modeling further preserved perturbation-induced coordination between modalities, including concordant peak-gene effects and cross-modal cellular neighborhood structure. These results establish MultiFlow as a unified generative framework for modeling paired molecular states and predicting their coordinated perturbation responses across cellular contexts. Code and tutorial of MultiFlow are available at https://github.com/liuq-lab/MultiFlow .

records.title: Prediction transfer does not imply reliability transfer in single-cell foundation models.
records.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are increasingly transferred across tissues, diseases, perturbation screens, and experimental platforms. Although substantial effort has focused on prediction transfer, it remains unclear whether a model's assessment of its own reliability transfers similarly across biological contexts. Here we define reliability transfer as the ability to transfer an accurate assessment of when model predictions are likely to be correct or incorrect and investigate its behavior across ten perturbation-prediction systems spanning multiple datasets, models, and evaluation settings. We find that reliability transfer varies substantially across source-target pairs and cannot be inferred from predictive performance alone, indicating that prediction transfer and reliability transfer constitute distinct forms of generalization. Analyses of biological annotations, network connectivity, target exposure, and contextual factors reveal that prediction reliability is associated with both shared and context-dependent signals, with their relative importance differing across systems. To characterize this variability, we introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints, context-level signatures derived from strictly cross-fitted SHAP explanations that summarize how reliability estimators combine biological and contextual information when assigning confidence. Across systems, contexts with similar attribution-magnitude fingerprints tended to transfer reliability more successfully, and fingerprint similarity identified transfer sources achieving higher reliability-transfer performance within the observed candidate set. However, these relationships weakened under stricter cross-family transfer settings, indicating that transferable reliability structure remains partly dependent on shared contextual information. Finally, transferred reliability estimators produced different perturbation rankings despite identical perturbation predictions, illustrating a practical consequence of reliability transfer for downstream prioritization. Together, these results establish reliability transfer as a distinct aspect of foundation-model generalization and introduce reliability-attribution fingerprints as a framework for characterizing transferable reliability structure across biological contexts.

records.title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
records.abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

records.title: The Tenocyte from Atom to Cell: A Critical Multiscale Synthesis Linking Collagen Chemistry, Tissue Mechanics, Cell Mechanobiology and Mathematical Modelling.
records.abstract: The tenocyte builds, maintains, senses and degrades one of the most mechanically demanding extracellular matrices in vertebrates, yet the chemical, physical, biological and mathematical descriptions of this system have developed in largely separate literatures. This review examines the tenocyte-matrix unit as a single causal system spanning eight orders of magnitude in length, organised around five transitions: from collagen chemistry to molecular mechanics; from molecule to fibril and fascicle; from tissue loading to the cellular mechanical stimulus; from stimulus to transcription; and from cellular output back to matrix composition. At each transition, we weigh competing hypotheses, identify where evidence is decisive and where it remains correlative, and state the governing equations. We integrate advances from 2021-2026, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of human tendons, the establishment of PIEZO1 as a causal regulator of tendon stiffness, and microstructurally derived constitutive models. We argue that tendon homeostasis is a closed-loop control problem, formalised as a mechanostat with an inverted-U dose-response, and that the recurrent pathologies of tendon-tendinopathy, ageing, diabetic stiffening and fibrotic healing are failures of this loop rather than of any single component. An open-source computational companion (tenocyte-virtual-cell) is introduced, and a prioritised research agenda closes the review.

records.title: Primary-Tumor Transcriptomic Signatures Associated with Circulating Tumor Cells Status in Breast Cancer: From CTC-Negative Remodeling to CTC-Associated Metastatic Programs.
records.abstract: Background/Objectives: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) play a central role in metastasis by enabling tumor dissemination through the bloodstream. However, the molecular transition from CTC-negative (CTC-) to CTC-positive (CTC+) states and their associated systemic remodeling remain poorly understood. Methods: We performed a transcriptomic comparison between CTC+, CTC-, and healthy individuals using RNA-seq data and a bioinformatics pipeline. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were subjected to functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, survival modeling, and drug perturbation prediction to delineate the molecular determinants of CTC emergence and persistence. Results: Primary tumors from CTC+ patients exhibited distinct transcriptomic profiles characterized by the upregulation of genes involved in PI3K-Akt signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and chromatin regulation (e.g., HDAC1, JUN, KLK10), alongside the downregulation of immune activation pathways, including complement, B-cell receptor (BCR), and T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling. Multi-gene survival models derived from upregulated (KLK10, MEOX2, IRS4, RND2) and downregulated (ALDH3A1, PPP2R2B, IGF1R) hub genes significantly stratified patient outcomes (HR = 1.74-2.44, p < 0.01). In contrast, primary tumors from CTC- patients displayed early systemic transcriptional alterations relative to healthy controls, with 1700+ DEGs linked to MAPK/ERK and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways, suggesting pre-metastatic immune reprogramming even before CTC detection. Drug repurposing analysis identified Trichostatin A, BX-795, and Alvocidib as candidate compounds capable of reversing the CTC+ transcriptional signature. Conclusions: Rather than supporting a strictly binary view of CTC status, our findings are consistent with a transcriptional continuum of distinct yet partially overlapping primary-tumor transcriptional states associated with CTC- and CTC+ status, highlighting a molecular shift from immune suppression to epigenetic adaptation that facilitates hematogenous dissemination. The identified multi-gene prognostic panels and small-molecule candidates provide a foundation for CTC-targeted therapeutic strategies and early detection biomarkers in breast cancer.

records.title: Design and validation of nucleosome binding peptides using BindCraft.
records.abstract: Chromatin is a sophisticated assembly of DNA, RNA and proteins in the nuclei of eukaryotic cells. Protein-protein interactions that govern chromatin function are key regulators of genome activity, making them prime targets for drug discovery. Engineering and modulating these contacts presents a viable pathway for innovative epigenetic therapies. Nucleosomes, the primary structural units of chromatin, feature various interaction interfaces, most notably the acidic patch. This region serves as a critical binding site for numerous chromatin-associated proteins, often via their intrinsically disordered regions. Advances in AI-driven protein design have recently opened new avenues for the rational development of molecules aimed at modulating these chromatin interactions. In this research, we implemented an integrated computational and experimental framework to design and validate peptides targeting the nucleosome acidic patch. We relied on the AI protein design approach implemented in BindCraft to design nucleosome binding peptides. To achieve precise quantitative analysis of these interactions, we refined a donor FRET quenching assay specifically for this application, enabling sensitive and consistent measurement of binding affinities for the designed sequences. We successfully identified peptides with high affinity for the acidic patch on canonical nucleosome core particles. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted design for chromatin-targeting agents and establish an effective workflow for their validation, laying the groundwork for synthetic epigenetic modulators and the broader use of protein design in managing 3D genome organization.

records.title: HydroGuard: a controlled release hydrogel-phage delivery system to combat catheter-associated urinary tract infections.
records.abstract: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) rank as the fourth-most significant nosocomial infection globally. CAUTIs account for approximately 80% of hospital-acquired urinary tract infections and represent nearly one-third of all device-associated infections. Urinary catheters serve as a hub for bacteria to form highly resistant biofilms containing pathogens, like Enterococcus (E.) faecalis that reduce effectiveness of the immune system and antibiotic treatments. Therefore, tackling biofilm formation at the catheter surface becomes a crucial step in mitigating CAUTIs. We aim to address E. faecalis biofilm formation by engineering HydroGuard: a Gelatin Methacryloyl (Gel-MA)-based hydrogel injected with bacteriophages, to provide targeted, enzyme-triggered antimicrobial activity. Enterococcus faecalis expresses gelatinase (GelE), a zinc metalloprotease that enhances biofilm formation. GelMA is susceptible to GelE-mediated degradation, enabling enzyme-triggered release of bacteriophages that specifically lyse E. faecalis. For a Biosafety Level 1 proof-of-concept experiment with a well-studied host and phage system, we heterologously expressed GelE in Escherichia (E.) coli DH5α to emulate native E. faecalis expression. This system was tested on dynamically grown biofilms, to simulate similar conditions to the urinary tract. Currently, the E. coli system has shown preliminary inhibition when tested against the hydrogel product, however testing of different phage combinations is needed. Mathematical modelling identified hydrogel crosslinking density as a critical tuneable parameter governing therapeutic availability and predicted nonlinear, degradation-dependent phage release profiles. Sensitivity analyses revealed design trade-offs between structural stability and antimicrobial responsiveness. Together, the biofilm, hydrogel, phage-bacteria, and protein design models form a multiscale computational framework that links biofilm development and environmental conditions to enzyme-mediated hydrogel degradation, phage release, and bacterial suppression. Agent-based biofilm simulations captured emergent spatial dynamics under nutrient, flow, and pH constraints, while a coupled predator-prey model investigated phage-bacteria population dynamics within the degrading GelMA matrix. Computational protein design further explored collagen-like peptide motifs with enhanced folding stability and preserved gelatinase cleavage sites, providing a molecular-level approach to tuneable degradation kinetics. This multiscale framework provides predictive insight into how biofilm conditions, hydrogel degradation, and phage availability interact within the proposed system, while the preliminary experimental observations provide supporting evidence for its feasibility. By integrating synthetic biology, tissue engineering, and modelling, HydroGuard offers a novel, non-antibiotic strategy for CAUTI prevention.

records.title: Function-preserving CD8⁺ T Cell Immunogenicity minimization through protein design.
records.abstract: Rapid advances in protein design enable new approaches in adoptive cell therapy, but foreign proteins can elicit cytotoxic T cell responses, and hence there is considerable need for approaches which reduce immunogenicity without compromising protein function. Here, we develop a computational framework integrating structure-guided sequence design with MHC class I epitope prediction to efficiently tune protein immunogenicity while preserving function. Using a de novo-designed luciferase as a model, we demonstrate epitope elimination while preserving function across 5 common mouse alleles and extend our computational optimization to 25 common human MHC-I alleles. In mice immunized with mRNA-lipid nanoparticles, variants designed to have few MHC-I epitopes elicited little detectable CD8⁺ T cell response, whereas variants designed to include multiple epitopes induced robust responses. Together, these results demonstrate that the CD8⁺ T cell immunogenicity of designed proteins can be tuned while preserving function, opening the door to incorporation of designed proteins in a next generation of adoptive cell therapies.

records.title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor.
records.abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the C-terminal IDR of the transcription factor RUNX2, which is required to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR motifs are dispensable; instead, the conformational dynamics of the IDR predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo . These findings extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

records.title: Phyfold: environment aware mathematical modeling for protein folding dynamics integrated with physics informed neural network.
records.abstract: Protein folding remains a fundamental problem in computational biology, where understanding folding trajectories and dynamic behavior under physiological conditions is critical for linking structure to function. Recent advances such as AlphaFold have revolutionized sequence to structure prediction, establishing a powerful and robust foundation for computational protein modeling. Building upon this success, we introduce a novel physics informed computational framework that expands static structure prediction toward dynamic and physically consistent modeling of protein folding processes. The proposed framework unifies a mathematically grounded reaction diffusion model of folding kinetics with deep sequence embeddings through a physics informed neural network (PINN), ensuring consistency with governing physical laws while remaining biologically grounded. We refer to this unified framework as PhyFold. Our results illustrate that the proposed approach effectively captures environment dependent folding dynamics and shows strong agreement with both numerical reference solutions and experimental fluorescence measurements under physiologically relevant conditions. By explicitly integrating environmental factors such as temperature, pressure, and pH, PhyFold enables realistic, physics aware simulation of protein folding dynamics. This approach offers a natural extension of modern structure prediction methods and opens new directions for protein design, structure guided drug discovery, and personalized medicine. The code to reproduce the work is available at https://github.com/jamshaidwarraich/PhyFold.git .Scientific contributionPhyFold introduces a hybrid Bio-Physics Informed Neural Network framework that models protein folding kinetics as a reaction diffusion partial differential equation with environmentally modulated kinetic coefficients, integrated with ProtT5 sequence embeddings for sequence specific spatiotemporal prediction an approach not previously demonstrated in the literature. Unlike purely data driven or static structure prediction methods, PhyFold explicitly encodes temperature, pH, and pressure dependence into governing kinetic coefficients, enabling physically interpretable simulation of cooperative folding transitions across diverse physiological conditions. Dual validation against finite difference reference solutions and experimental GFP fluorescence measurements confirms mathematical consistency and biological relevance, establishing PhyFold as a computationally efficient surrogate for environment aware protein folding dynamics.

records.title: An educational activity tailored for undergraduate students on AI-driven nanobody design for targeted antiviral therapeutics.
records.abstract: Protein-based biologics are converging at an unprecedented pace as generative artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes early-stage drug discovery. Nanobodies, single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid heavy chain-only immunoglobulins, are an emerging class of antiviral biologics prized for their small size, stability, and access to cryptic viral epitopes. Traditional nanobody discovery relies on animal immunization and phage display screening, a process that can take 6 to 12 months and is entirely inaccessible within a standard undergraduate laboratory session. Here, we describe a succinct, in silico-based laboratory activity that uses a generative AI protein design server, GeoFlow-V3 (https://prot.design/), to allow undergraduate students to design a novel antiviral nanobody against the influenza A virus (IAV) hemagglutinin (HA) protein. This activity builds on our group's prior use of generative AI for undergraduate siRNA design teaching and extends the same pedagogical model to structural protein engineering. To our knowledge, this is the first use of a generative AI protein design platform for teaching nanobody design at the undergraduate level.

records.title: Liquid biopsy in genitourinary cancers: circulating tumor DNA as a predictive biomarker for treatment selection and resistance monitoring.
records.abstract: Genitourinary (GU) cancers-prostate, urothelial, and renal cell carcinomas (RCCs)-are a leading source of oncologic morbidity and mortality. Tumor heterogeneity and evolving resistance limit static tissue biopsies, requiring real-time, non-invasive biomarkers. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) captures the tumor's mutational landscape in real time and has emerged as a candidate biomarker for treatment selection and resistance monitoring in GU malignancies. An integrative review was conducted by two independent reviewers following the Whittemore and Knafl integrative review framework, informed by PRISMA 2020 conventions. Searches covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Embase, and Web of Science (January 2020-April 2026). Screening and extraction were performed independently by both reviewers, with disagreements resolved by consensus. After deduplication, 118 records were screened, 39 assessed in full text, and 15 studies met inclusion criteria, stratified by cancer site. ctDNA functions primarily as a prognostic and treatment-monitoring biomarker across GU malignancies, with predictive utility for treatment selection well established in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) and still maturing elsewhere. In castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), ctDNA tumor fraction (TF) at enzalutamide cycle 3 independently predicts progression-free and overall survival (OS; median OS 16.0 vs. 22.1 months, ctDNA-detected vs. -undetected with discordant prostate-specific antigen). In MIBC, post-cystectomy ctDNA identifies relapse with 94% sensitivity and 98% specificity, and a ctDNA-stratified IMvigor010 analysis reveals an OS benefit from adjuvant atezolizumab [hazard ratio (HR) 0.59] in ctDNA-positive patients only. In RCC, the least mature stratum, cfDNA quantity, TP53 mutation, TF, and BAP1 status are associated with survival on systemic therapy. In upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC), perioperative ctDNA fraction predicts recurrence-free survival, with clonal haematopoiesis accounting for a notable share of false positives. ctDNA is a molecularly grounded biomarker with the strongest evidence in metastatic CRPC (mCRPC) and MIBC, an expanding but preliminary base in RCC, and limited capacity, outside MIBC, to guide treatment selection.

records.title: Spatial and single-cell insights into the prostate cancer microenvironment: overcoming immunotherapy resistance through multidimensional strategies.
records.abstract: Despite breakthroughs in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) across various malignancies, prostate cancer (PCa), particularly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), has shown limited responses to ICIs. This pervasive primary resistance is fundamentally driven by the canonically "immune-cold" and highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of PCa. Propelled by recent advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, this review comprehensively deconstructs the dynamic spatiotemporal evolution of the PCa immune landscape across localized, mCRPC, and lineage-plastic variant stages (e.g., neuroendocrine and double-negative PCa). We systematically delineate how the profound immune-excluded phenotype is sculpted not by isolated events, but by an intricate, multicellular suppressive ecosystem. Specifically, we detail the subclonal heterogeneity, spatial topography, and metabolic crosstalk of key suppressive populations, including specific tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subsets, regulatory T cells (Tregs), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Furthermore, we elucidate the tumor-intrinsic genetic aberrations (e.g., PTEN inactivation, TP53 mutations) and epigenetic rewiring (e.g., EZH2, CHD1, ARID1A dysregulation) that initiate and perpetually orchestrate this suppressive network. Finally, we highlight emerging therapeutic vulnerabilities and future translational directions. Dismantling the microenvironmental barriers in PCa necessitates transcending singular ICI blockade by employing novel combinatorial strategies that target chemotactic recruitment axes (e.g., CXCR2/CXCR4), reverse metabolic plasticity, and abrogate epigenetic silencing. Coupled with high-resolution liquid biopsy biomarkers (e.g., ctDNA, B7-H3+ EVs) for precise patient stratification and cutting-edge synthetic biology interventions, these multidimensional approaches hold profound promise for reversing the dual metabolic and immune suppressive state of PCa, thereby overcoming clinical immunotherapy resistance.

records.title: Ribosomal RNA-derived fragments in cancer: molecular identity, cellular context, and functional evidence.
records.abstract: Ribosomal RNA-derived fragments (rRFs), also termed rRNA-derived small RNAs (rsRNAs), occur in cells and biofluids, but their detection does not establish biological activity. This review systematically summarizes current research on rRF biogenesis, intracellular functions, extracellular localization and carriage, and clinical associations, while emphasizing that the detection of rRFs does not in itself establish biological function. Stress-associated cleavage, candidate-specific non-canonical processing, and extracellular ribosome fragmentation can each contribute to the observed repertoire. Functional cancer studies remain concentrated in a few candidates: depletion of a 28S-derived rRF3 affects H1299 cell phenotypes; rsRNA-28S inhibition increases PTGIS expression and taxane resistance in prostate-cancer cells; and synthetic gastric-cancer S2 and S7 mimics alter target reporters and protein abundance. These findings do not establish a common rRF pathway or therapeutic efficacy. Tissue and circulating signatures show diagnostic or prognostic associations, including a methylation-sensitive 28S fragment assay, but many cohorts are small and lack prospective external validation. Therapeutic development could test inhibition of a confirmed tumor-promoting fragment or replacement of a protective fragment, provided that endogenous function, selectivity over parental rRNA, delivery, and safety are established. Overall, rRFs show emerging biological and biomarker potential in cancer, but their clinical translation will require stronger mechanistic validation, prospective clinical evidence, and rigorous assessment of delivery and safety.

records.title: CLDN18.2 in colorectal mucinous adenocarcinoma: a lineage-associated biomarker and emerging translational target.
records.abstract: Colorectal mucinous adenocarcinoma (CMA) is a histologically and molecularly distinct subtype of colorectal cancer (CRC), marked by abundant extracellular mucin, a predilection for the proximal colon, and frequent overlap with deficient mismatch repair/high microsatellite instability (dMMR/MSI-H), BRAF V600E mutation, CpG island methylator phenotype-high (CIMP-high) status, and serrated pathway biology. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors and molecularly targeted therapies have expanded treatment options for selected patients with advanced CRC, treatment strategies tailored to the histologic phenotype, lineage programs, and microenvironmental architecture of CMA remain limited. CLDN18.2, the gastric isoform encoded by CLDN18, is now a clinically validated therapeutic target in gastric and gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinomas. Recent pathology-based studies suggest that CLDN18.2 expression is uncommon in unselected conventional colorectal adenocarcinoma but enriched in CMA, mucin-rich CRC, and tumors with gastric-type or foregut-like differentiation, particularly those arising in the proximal colon or harboring dMMR/MSI-H status or BRAF V600E mutation. This pattern suggests that CLDN18.2 in CMA is unlikely to be a classic oncogenic driver; instead, it is better viewed as a therapeutically accessible, lineage-associated membrane antigen. This review summarizes the biological rationale, expression data, companion diagnostic issues, therapeutic platforms, and translational barriers relevant to CLDN18.2 in CMA. We propose a framework centered on lineage reprogramming, antigen enrichment, assay standardization, and therapeutic translation. Current evidence supports CLDN18.2 as a candidate biomarker for biomarker-enriched investigation, not as an established therapeutic target in CMA. Future work should prioritize CMA-specific preclinical models, standardized membranous immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring, and prospective trials that integrate CLDN18.2 expression with molecular subtype and tumor microenvironmental features.

records.title: AAV serotype IVDs for patient selection in gene therapy development: Technical and regulatory considerations by ARDAT consortium.
records.abstract: Currently, most clinical trials for adeno-associated virus (AAV)-based gene therapy (GT) exclude patients with pre-existing anti-AAV antibodies (AAV Abs) due to potential impact on treatment efficacy and safety. Diagnostic regulations require sponsors to define pre-existing AAV Ab level cutoffs and validate patient selection assays before beginning clinical studies. In the absence of robust clinical outcome data early in development, sponsors often rely on thresholds derived from literature or preclinical studies, or default to assay detection limits. The transferability of these thresholds to actual clinical outcomes remains uncertain, leading sponsors to use conservative cutoffs to avoid costly revalidations and development delays. This may prevent some patients from accessing potentially beneficial treatments. We advocate for more flexible validation approaches based on current understanding of antibody characteristics and the commonly used assay formats. We propose an AAV serotype-specific in vitro diagnostic (IVD) assay, an "AAV serotype IVD," with pragmatic analytical validations for single AAV serotypes. This approach would allow sponsors to establish clinically meaningful cutoffs through adaptive clinical trials that progressively include patients with escalating pre-existing AAV Ab levels by implementing multiple cutoffs during clinical development. These measures could expedite AAV GT development while expanding access for patients with elevated pre-existing AAV Ab levels.

records.title: Exploration of circulating proteins associated with tumor stromal content using matched serum and tissue samples from patients with colon cancer.
records.abstract: Liquid biopsies provide a source of biomolecules that allow tumor characterization. Increasing evidence shows that the tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a central role in behavior of colon cancer. This study assessed which proteins in the circulation correlate with tumor stromal content through analysis of serum and corresponding tissue samples from patients with colon cancer. A broad set of circulating proteins is quantified, ranging from common apolipoproteins, transport and complement factors, to key factors from interconnected stromal pathways such as coagulation and acute phase inflammation. The cohort consisted of 97 patients with colon cancer and 50 control individuals who all underwent colonoscopy. Targeted mass spectrometry was applied to quantify 156 serum proteins via their surrogate peptides and corresponding internal standards. Matching solid tumor tissue slides from all 97 patients were used to determine the Tumor-Stroma Ratio (TSR). Serum protein levels were compared between stroma-high and stroma-low tumors, resulting in a subset of discriminating proteins. Composite protein scores were evaluated in multivariable Cox models. Four serum proteins differed significantly between stroma-high and stroma-low tumors, all showing elevated levels in stroma-high patients, including complement-related proteins (C2, factor B, and C1r subcomponent-like protein) and the coagulation-related vitamin K-dependent protein S. This resulted in a composite Stromal Protein Score that may capture TME-driven variations. The Stromal Protein Score was significantly different between stroma-high and stroma-low patients (adjusted p < 0.001). Our data indicate that stroma-high tumors are associated with systemic alterations in complement and coagulation-related proteins. The results encourage further development of liquid biopsy-based protein profiling approaches, aiming for clinical implementation as a non-invasive strategy for TME-informed risk stratification and treatment monitoring in colon cancer.
